b) What will be the expected population 10 years from now?

Option 1: Borrow the money at \(10\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly for the full term.
Option 2: Borrow the money at \(12\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly for 5 years and then renegotiate the loan based on the new balance for the last 5 years.
If, in 5 years, the interest rate will be \(6\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly, how much will Serena save by choosing the second option?

Plan A: \(10\%/\mathrm{a}\) simple interest for 2 years
Plan B: \(5\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly for 2 years
Which plan should she choose? Justify your answer.
Eric bought a $1000 Canada Savings Bond that earns \(5\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded annually. Eric can redeem the bond in 7 years. Determine the future value of the bond.

Dieter deposits $9000 into an account that pays \(10\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly. After three years, the interest rate changes to \(9\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded semi-annually. Calculate the value of his investment two years after this change.

Cliff has some money he wants to invest for his retirement. He is offered two options:

\(10\%/\mathrm{a}\) simple interest
\(5\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded annually
Under what conditions should he choose the first option?

You are searching different banks for the best interest rate on an investment, and you find these rates:

\(6.6\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded annually
\(6.55\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded semi-annually
\(6.5\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly
\(6.45\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded monthly

Bernie deposited $4000 into an account that pays \(4\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded quarterly during the first year. The interest rate on this account is then increased by \(0.2\%\) each year. Calculate the balance in Bernie’s account after three years.

On the day Rachel was born, her grandparents deposited $500 into a savings account that earns \(4.8\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded monthly. They deposited the same amount on her 5th, 10th, and 15th birthdays. Determine the balance in the account on Rachel’s 18th birthday.

a) The interest rate is \(18\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded monthly. What was the selling price of the player?

a) Calculate the monthly payment for each term.

b) How much would they save in interest by choosing the shorter term?

c) What other factors should the Pecas consider before making their financing decision?

Charles would like to buy a new car that costs $32\,000. The dealership offers to finance the car at \(2.4\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded monthly for five years with monthly payments. The dealer will reduce the selling price by $3000 if Charles pays cash. Charles can get a loan from his bank at \(5.4\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded monthly. Which is the best way to buy the car? Justify your answer with calculations.

a) Determine the monthly payment for each term.

b) Calculate how much interest Nina would pay in each case.

a) What was the selling price of the stereo?

b) How much interest will Pedro have paid over the term of the loan?

If Leo has 20 years until he retires and wants to use the investment for recreation for the first 10 years of retirement, what is the maximum quarterly withdrawal he can make?

Charmaine calculates that she will require about $2500 per month for the first 15 years of her retirement. If she has 25 years until she retires, how much should she invest each month at \(9\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded monthly for the next 25 years if she plans to withdraw $2500 per month for the 15 years after that?

Option A: $1000 each week for life
Option B: $660\,000 in one lump sum
The current interest rate is \(6.76\%/\mathrm{a}\) compounded weekly.

a) Which option would you suggest to a winner who expects to live for another 25 years?

b) When is option A better than option B?

Stefan claims that he has found a different method for calculating the present value of an annuity. Instead of calculating the present value of each payment, he calculates the future value of each payment. Then he calculates the sum of the future values of the payments. Finally, he calculates the present value of this total sum.

a) Use Stefan’s method to solve Example 1 (a).

b) Create another example to show that his claim is true. Include timelines.

c) Use the formula for present value to prove that Stefan’s claim works for all annuities.

Check (a): Ordinary PV of annuity: \(PV = 500\dfrac{1-(1.083)^{-10}}{0.083} \approx \$3310.11\). Stefan’s FV-then-discount approach yields the same present value.
